opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the way to think about it is that pre-training gives you this incredibly rich base of representations almost for free. You're training on basically the whole internet, trillions of tokens, and to predict the next token well you have to learn a huge amount about the world. Grammar first, then facts, then increasingly abstract stuff: how arguments work, how code works, how people reason, what someone is likely to do next. Next-token prediction sounds dumb, but to get really good at it you end up having to model the process that generated the text, and that process is humans thinking.

So the advantage is that you start from something that already has a broad world model and a lot of latent capabilities, and then post-training, RLHF, instruction tuning, RL on reasoning, is much more about unlocking and shaping those capabilities than creating them from scratch. A lot of what people call "unhobbling" is exactly this. The raw capability is sitting in the base model, and the question is whether you can get it out. Chain-of-thought is a good example. It's not that the model suddenly learned math; you just let it actually think before answering.

The other thing is that it's general in a way narrow approaches never were. With AlphaGo-style systems you had to build an environment and a reward signal for each domain. Pre-training sidesteps that. Human text covers every domain, so you get transfer across all of them, and you see the capabilities scale pretty smoothly with compute. That's the crucial empirical fact: you put in more compute and data and the loss goes down predictably, and with it you get these qualitative jumps, GPT-2 to GPT-4 being roughly preschooler to smart high schooler.

Now, the open question is the data wall. We're running out of high-quality internet text, and so the next phase is figuring out how to keep getting the benefits. That might be synthetic data, self-play, RL, or more sample-efficient algorithms, closer to how a human reads a textbook and actually works through it, rather than just skimming a trillion tokens. But I'd argue the base that pre-training gives you is what makes all of that possible. You need that general foundation before RL has anything to bootstrap from.

r002.rationale: It links the broad world model and latent capabilities built during pre-training to transfer across domains.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the way to understand it is that pre-training is basically the most efficient way we've found to compress all of human knowledge into a model, and the thing that's surprising is how much general capability falls out of that. You're just predicting the next token on the internet, but to do that well you have to implicitly learn a huge amount: world models, reasoning, how code works, how people argue. So you get this very broad base of intelligence almost for free, in the sense that you didn't have to specify any of it by hand.

The advantage over, say, pure reinforcement learning from scratch is enormous. If you tried to teach a model to do math or write code only through RL, you'd be searching in this gigantic space with a terribly sparse reward signal. Pre-training gives you a prior that's already in the right neighborhood. The model already "knows" what a proof looks like, what a bug looks like. Then RL or post-training is more like unlocking and sharpening capabilities that are latently there rather than building them from nothing. That's why a relatively small amount of fine-tuning compute can produce such dramatic changes in behavior.

And I think the other piece is that the scaling story on pre-training has been remarkably smooth. You pour in more compute and more data, and the loss goes down predictably, and the downstream capabilities keep improving in ways that, to be fair, were often surprising on the specifics but very consistent in the trend. That predictability is itself an advantage. It lets labs plan multi-billion-dollar clusters with some confidence that the model on the other end will actually be better.

The caveat I'd add is that pre-training alone is "unhobbled" only so far. The raw base model is kind of like a brilliant person who's read everything but has no idea what you want from them and can't plan over long horizons. So the advantage of pre-training is the foundation. The question for the next few years is how far you can go in building the scaffolding, the agency, the test-time compute on top of that foundation, and I think that's where a lot of the action is.

astra-6.text:
I think the key thing pre-training gives you is this enormous amount of background knowledge that you can bring to bear on a new problem. You’re not starting from scratch every time. You’ve learned something about language, about code, about how people reason, about how the world works, and a lot of those things transfer.

If you think about what makes a human useful at a task, it’s often not just the specific training they received for that task. It’s all the other things they learned over the preceding twenty years. You can give someone a fairly short explanation of a new job because you’re building on this huge foundation.

Pre-training gives models something analogous. And the interesting question is how far that transfer goes. Are you learning a collection of patterns that work in familiar situations, or are you learning more general mechanisms for figuring things out? I think the remarkable thing is how much generality you get from what looks like a very simple objective: predict the next token. To do that well across all these different domains, you end up having to learn a lot of the underlying structure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the remarkable thing about pre-training is that you get this enormous amount of learning before you ever have to act in the world. A human has to acquire knowledge over a lifetime, with a pretty limited stream of experience. A model can absorb patterns from an enormous fraction of humanity’s recorded knowledge.

And to predict that text well, it can’t just memorize facts. It has to learn something about the processes that generated the text: how people reason, how the world works, what happens when you run a piece of code. The training objective is simple, but doing it really well pushes you toward increasingly general capabilities.

Now, that doesn’t mean pre-training automatically gives you an agent that can go off and do somebody’s job. There’s a difference between having the underlying knowledge and being able to reliably apply it over a long sequence of actions. But it gives you this extraordinarily rich starting point. When you train the model on a new task, you’re often eliciting and recombining capabilities it already has, rather than teaching it everything from scratch.

That’s the central advantage: you can amortize this huge investment in learning across an enormous range of tasks. You don’t need a separate system, trained from zero, for every new problem.
